issues.legal_issue: A High Court should give brief reasons when summarily dismissing an appeal involving genuinely plausible competing interpretations of written instruments.
material_facts: The High Court summarily dismissed an appeal concerning the construction of written instruments.
The High Court had called for the record to check whether the trial court's decree was legal and proper.
The competing interpretations of the instruments had more than mere plausibility.
issues.conclusion: The High Court ought to have given a brief statement of reasons for dismissing the appeal summarily.
issues.legal_principle: In appeals involving construction of written instruments where rival interpretations have more than mere plausibility, a High Court should briefly state its reasons even when dismissing summarily. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this practice rule.

predicates.high_court_summary_appeal: The High Court summarily dismissed an appeal from a trial court decision.
predicates.plausible_competing_instrument_interpret: The parties advanced competing interpretations of written instruments, and each interpretation had more than mere plausibility.
predicates.record_called_for_review: The High Court called for the record to check whether the trial court's decision was legal and proper.

issues.definition: When a High Court summarily dismisses an appeal after reviewing the record and the appeal presents plausible competing interpretations of written instruments, it should give brief reasons.

issues.legal_issue: A person cannot protect possession under the doctrine of part performance without satisfying its requirements for a written contract, ascertainable transfer terms, possession in part performance, and willingness to perform.
material_facts: The person initially defended a possession suit on the ground that he was a tenant and later sought to add a defense based on an alleged agreement of sale.
The application to amend the defense was made after the tenancy proceedings had ended and was rejected as belated and mala fide.
There was no written contract of sale signed by the owner; a letter from the owner's brother referred to an alleged oral agreement.
The letter did not set out terms sufficient to ascertain the transfer with reasonable certainty.
The person obtained possession under a power of attorney as an agent, and the evidence did not show that the character of his possession changed.
He continued at intervals to pay the owner the agreed annual sum, a course of conduct inconsistent with possession as a prospective purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The person was not entitled to protect his possession under section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act requires a written contract signed by or on behalf of the transferor, terms from which the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty, possession taken or continued in part performance of that contract, an act in furtherance where applicable, and willingness by the transferee to perform. A letter that is only written evidence of an oral sale agreement is not the written contract itself. No earlier case is relied on.

rule.if: possession_defense_proceeding and (late_new_sale_defense or no_signed_written_sale_contract or uncertain_sale_terms or possession_not_under_sale_contract or conduct_inconsistent_with_purchaser_status)

predicates.possession_defense_proceeding: A person facing a claim for possession relies on an alleged sale agreement as a defense to remaining in possession.
predicates.late_new_sale_defense: The person sought to introduce the sale-agreement defense only after pursuing a different defense through separate proceedings.
predicates.no_signed_written_sale_contract: There was no written sale contract signed by the owner or on the owner's behalf.
predicates.uncertain_sale_terms: The written material did not state terms from which the proposed transfer could be ascertained with reasonable certainty.
predicates.possession_not_under_sale_contract: The person obtained possession under an agency arrangement, and the evidence did not show that possession later changed character under a sale agreement.
predicates.conduct_inconsistent_with_purchaser_stat: The person continued to make payments to the owner on terms inconsistent with possession as a purchaser.

issues.definition: A person defending possession on an alleged sale cannot obtain protection when the defense was introduced late or the written agreement, its terms, the basis for possession, or the person's conduct fails to meet the stated predicates.

issues.legal_issue: A power of attorney is not a sham or colorable document merely because a recital about possession is inaccurate or the instrument's practical purpose differs from its expressed purpose, where the instrument was intended to be acted on and was acted on.
material_facts: The power of attorney stated that the owner was in possession, although other persons were actually occupying the land without authority.
Its practical purpose was to enable the agent to obtain possession from those occupants.
The agent promptly wrote to the owner accepting the power's terms, including the arrangement for annual payments and retention of the remainder of income as remuneration.
The agent acted under the power and continued making the agreed payments.
issues.conclusion: The power of attorney was not a sham or colorable document; it was intended to be acted on and was in fact acted on.
issues.legal_principle: An inaccurate recital or a difference between an instrument's expressed purpose and its practical purpose does not, by itself, make the instrument sham or colorable when the parties intended it to operate and acted on it. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.power_of_attorney_dispute: A party disputes whether an authority instrument was genuine or merely a sham.
predicates.instrument_terms_accepted: The agent communicated acceptance of the authority instrument's terms to the principal.
predicates.instrument_actually_implemented: The agent acted under the instrument and carried out its arrangement with the principal.

issues.definition: An authority instrument is not a sham or colorable when its terms were accepted and the parties implemented it, despite an inaccurate recital or a different practical purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A person who made improvements while acting as a tenant or prospective purchaser, rather than as a licensee, cannot claim irrevocability of a licence based on those improvements.
material_facts: The person argued that he should be treated as a licensee and that permanent works and heavy expenses made the licence irrevocable.
The argument was based on treating the power of attorney as nominal, but the court found that it was intended to be acted on and was acted on.
The evidence did not adequately establish the improvements or expenses.

Even assuming permanent work had been done, the person did it in the belief that he was a tenant who could become a statutory purchaser or that an alleged sale would be completed, not in reliance on a licence.
issues.conclusion: The person could not rely on section 60(b) of the Easements Act to make a licence irrevocable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60(b) of the Easements Act applies where a licensee, acting upon the licence, executes work of a permanent character and incurs expenses. Work done in the capacity of a tenant or prospective purchaser is not work done acting upon a licence. No earlier case is relied on.

predicates.irrevocable_license_claim: A person claims that a licence became irrevocable because the person made permanent improvements at expense.
predicates.work_done_as_tenant_or_potential_purchas: The person did the work believing that the person was a tenant or prospective purchaser, rather than acting in reliance on a licence.

issues.definition: A person claiming irrevocability based on permanent work cannot rely on that work when it was done as a tenant or prospective purchaser rather than in reliance on a licence.

issues.legal_issue: A person who did not preserve a claim for the value of improvements and relies only on capacities in which that value is unavailable cannot prevent an award of possession together with the improvements.
material_facts: The trial court was asked to award possession of the land, but no issue or argument was raised there that possession should not include the improvements.
The person's asserted capacities were tenant and possessor in part performance of an alleged sale.
The court found that the tenancy and part-performance claims failed and that neither capacity entitled him to the value of the alleged improvements.
issues.conclusion: The award of possession together with the improvements was not displaced by the person's claim to their value.
issues.legal_principle: A claim for the value of improvements cannot succeed on capacities that do not confer such a right; the court also noted that the issue had not been raised in the trial court. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.possession_decree_appeal: A person appeals from a decree awarding possession of property to another person.
predicates.improvement_value_issue_not_preserved: The person did not raise before the trial court an issue that possession should not be awarded together with the improvements.
predicates.asserted_statuses_do_not_support_compens: The person relies on statuses such as tenant or purchaser in part performance that do not entitle the person to the value of the improvements.

issues.definition: A person cannot defeat a possession award that includes improvements when the compensation issue was not preserved and the asserted statuses do not support compensation.

issues.legal_issue: An agent cannot recover improvement expenses under the agent's lien provision when the expenses were incurred without reference to the principal and do not fall within the provision's specified amounts.
material_facts: The person relied on section 221 of the Contract Act to claim amounts spent improving the principal's property.
The alleged expenditures were made without any reference to the principal.
The amounts were not shown to be commission, disbursements, or services in respect of property received by the agent.
issues.conclusion: The alleged improvement expenses were not recoverable under section 221 of the Contract Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 221 of the Contract Act gives an agent a lien over the principal's property received by the agent for amounts due as commission, disbursements, and services in respect of that property. It does not cover the alleged improvement expenses in this case. No earlier case is relied on.

predicates.agent_expense_recovery_claim: An agent seeks to recover expenses by relying on a lien over the principal's property.
predicates.expenses_incurred_without_principal_refe: The agent incurred the expenses without reference to the principal.
predicates.expenses_outside_agent_lien_categories: The expenses were not shown to be commission, disbursements, or services in respect of property received by the agent.

issues.definition: An agent cannot recover expenses through a lien when the expenses were incurred without reference to the principal and fall outside the categories described by the rule's predicates.

issues.legal_issue: A money award for unpaid agreed annual payments is not infirm merely because the parties had no general accounting relationship.
material_facts: The principal sought the amount due because the agent had failed to pay the agreed annual sum for certain years.
The trial court found that an amount remained due under the parties' written payment arrangement.
The agent challenged the money award on the ground that there had been no accountability between the parties.
issues.conclusion: The money award was not infirm, and the finding that the amount was due was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A claim for unpaid sums required by an agreed payment arrangement may support an award for the amount found due even if there was no general accounting relationship between the parties. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on.

predicates.appeal_from_money_award: A party appeals from a court's award of money to another party.
predicates.agreed_periodic_payments: The parties agreed that one party would make recurring payments to the other.
predicates.payments_found_unpaid: The court found that some of the agreed payments had not been paid.

issues.definition: An award for agreed recurring payments is upheld when the appeal concerns a money award and the court found that agreed payments remained unpaid.
